Grade 9 Certificate

By: Sophia Phirippides | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
A General Education Certificate at the end of Grade 9 has educators polarised, highlighting a system that is fundamentally broken at the core. Will this certificate add value to our children’s futur

Unique Selling Point:
By the end of July 2020 the field trial for the general education certificate at the end of Grade 9 is scheduled for completion. Not an exit strategy for learners according to the Department of Education, rather opening the options for non academic streams as well as setting an earlier national benchmark for learners before they get to Grade 12. But can this certificate enhance a failing educational system in dire need of attention?

Summary:
A Grade 9 certificate for South African learners is on the horizon. It is meant to create alternative learning streams for pupils not necessarily wanting to follow an academic outcome for their education, as well as providing an early national benchmark making schools accountable in earlier grades. This is modelled on the German schooling system, but South Africa has very different challenges when it comes to education infrastructure and industry participation which forms a large part of the German model.

A recent study has outlined fundamental failings within our education system with; 20% absenteeism of teachers on Mondays and Fridays, rising to 33% at every month-end, in schools serving predominantly poor black children only an average of 3.5 hours per school day is spent teaching compared to 6.5 hours in the middle and upper-class schools.
According to critics of the new certificate, many challenges across the country, including the observation that Grade 4 children have not yet learned to read with meaning need to be addressed before a grade 9 certificate enters our educational framework.

In addition, many educators say that this Grade 9 certificate is going to be costly to implement, in terms of infrastructure, implementation and resources - including supplying teachers who are skilled enough to teach the myriad of new subjects that will be introduced into schools. With the introduction of these subjects it may even be duplicating what the system has currently in place, in terms of the TVET colleges that are supposed to accommodate the non academic stream towards a National Certificate. On the other hand, the Department believes that this certificate will give more credence to the TVET qualifications.

Is the new Grade 9 certificate a deflection from the perception that, educationally, South Africa is moving backwards?

Further information:
We explore the pros and cons of this certificate whilst highlighting the plight of many young people as they face the crossroads of their academic pathway when they reach Grade 9. Do they continue to struggle on with an academic pathway if they are not doing well at school or do they choose the vocation or occupational streams that will now provide new options for them?

Professor Allais believes that the option of a non academic pathway that is being presented as a serious option is not the answer. She says that, because we are educating our children poorly we are creating options, such that, we don’t have to get the fundamentals of our educational system right first. If pupils were being taught properly to start off with then these would not necessarily be options they would follow. According to her, the world trend is to move away from an early certification.

Professor Stephanie Allais is fundamentally opposed to the Grade 9 certificate and is afraid that as a consequence, learners may take the easy way out of the school system, or be forced to follow alternative streams if their marks do not meet the grade, meaning we are not giving many learners a chance to improve their circumstance. According to her it perpetuates the cycle of poverty and class differentiation. She also says that for a model like this to work as it does in Germany and even Sweden, there needs to be industry involvement with curriculum setting and provision of apprenticeships and jobs. In South Africa we are nowhere near that.

Dr Ramphele asserts, “The question we should be asking ourselves as a society is why after 25 years of poor quality education outcomes we are still struggling to confront the root causes of this tragedy? Is there perhaps a mindset that propels us to have low expectations of our children, our teachers and ourselves?”

We also speak to two schools, Randburg Hoerskool and Klipspruit. Kipspruit has been at the brink of closing down, and with community involvement by a local group they have organised a course where the pupils are exposed to alternative career paths in a vocational and occupational sense. They did this to inspire learners to continue with their studies and not drop out of school. This is the department’s argument that, because there is such a high drop-out rate before Grade 12, this 3 tiered streaming will encourage pupils to stay in school.

We interview a young TVET graduate, who is still battling to find work and, along with 7 siblings, lives with his grandmother who is a teacher.

We speak to a Grade 9 pupil who is at the point of choosing their way forward. He wants to follow a non academic path but his mother is adamant that he has to do an academic matric.

We also speak to a pupil who attended the 7 week Klipspruit workshop and get some insight into how it changed the way they perceive their options after finishing school, now that they have been exposed to vocational and occupational subjects. Richard De Jongh is the initiator of this workshop and an example of how community intervention can play a role in changing a school’s outcomes. We also get to speak to the principal of Klipspruit.

At Randburg Hoerskool, we will get the alternative narrative of a school with more means and speak to the principal, Pieter Booysen on what the Grade 9 certificate will mean to a more academically inclined school and it’s pupils.

Dr Ramphele poses some solution and issues that need to be addressed first. She gives examples of community involvement as well as looking at performance based pay for teachers, which has worked well in places like India and Singapore, so that we start improving the system at the core. Home language based education needs to be part of the way forward, and improving literacy and numeracy at early grades.

According to Professor Allais who has been monitoring the progress of this Grade 9 certificate for the last two years, there has been very little discussion and participation from the DBE with regards to exploring the certificate’s merits prior to implementation. We challenge the Department and try to get some clarity on the burning issues.

Andrea Willoughby (Gr 9c)
Elgin Andrews (Gr 9a)
Lindokhule Nunu
Wanne Andrews (Gr 11)

Press Release:


The department of basic education is preparing a radical reform of secondary schooling to open up alternative career choices. South African Grade 9 learners will soon be able to obtain a general education certificate – can the GEC launch young people on fulfilling technical career paths?

Script:


Elgin: I love cooking and I want to become a chef.

VO: Elgin Andrews is a 14 year old grade 9 pupil. He lives in an informal settlement in Klipspruit West with his parents who are unemployed.

Elgin: I love working with my hands. I believe I can do many things. I can cook anything you want me to cook

VO: Elgin dreams of leaving school after Grade 9 to become a chef, through a TVET college that gives Technical and Vocational Education and Training. His mother Juanita has different ideas.

Juanita: For me I wouldn't want him to go out of school just with the grade 9 because I've got a matric. But if he does not have academics behind him, what does he have to fall back on?

LINK:
By the end of July 2020 the field trial for the general education certificate for Grade 9 is scheduled for completion.

Juanita: I don't agree with it at all. I'm like Grade 9, no child of mine is leaving.

Mac: You like this is not happening.

Juanita: Not at all, not on my watch.

LINK:
The Department of Education says it's not an exit strategy for learners. Rather it will open up options for non-academic streams and set an earlier benchmark for learners before matric. But can the certificate enhance a failing educational system in dire need of attention?

Dr Ramphele: We need to confront the root causes of why we register 1.2 million children in the grade R, not caught and only about half of that number ends up writing the final examination.

VO: Dr Mamphela Ramphele, a veteran educator, has played a leading role in many aspects of a transforming South Africa.

Dr Ramphele: We know that our children at Grade 9 level cannot compete with other children a grade eight in Africa. So the problems are humongous of our inability to teach our children to read with meaning, to write in a sensible way and to be able to compute. Grade 9 certificate is not going to do it.

VO: But for the Department of Basic Education, the Grade 9 General Education Certificate is not about sending children home to do nothing – rather it's about introducing three learning pathways that provide other career options and a recognised qualification prior to matric. The DBE’s Dr Moses Simelane emphasises the GEC is just the start of restructuring secondary education.

Dr Simelane: We will be introducing these different pathways; the academic which has always been there, the technical vocational learning pathway which we are reintroducing as an educational system the third one is the technical occupational pathway.

VO: Still in pilot phase, the goal is to implement the certificate by 2022 along with a cost-effective online marking system. The results will be used as a standardised benchmark and a guide for Grade 9 learners to choose the best stream for their particular aptitudes.

LINK:
It's all good and well that the department wants to introduce these two streams of vocational and occupational learning. But how sure are we that they are aligned to an already overstretched job market.

VO: Matriculant Lindo Nunu studied boiler making at a TVET college in False Bay. Unable to find a job on his return to Johannesburg, he's now enrolled at another college to improve his qualifications.

Mac: Did you always know you want to do boiler making

Lindo: No I didn’t. It was a last minute option

VO: Lindo really wanted to be a mechanical engineer but – like Elgin - is one of many students who may not get to follow their dream careers, because of subject choices.

Juanita: My son, I know the potential that he has. So what this is actually saying to him is that he can settle for less.

VO: Director of the Centre for Research and Labour at Wits University, Professor Stephanie Allais has monitored the progress of this initiative for two years and criticizes the DBE for not releasing enough information.

Stephanie: If you're going to massify technical and vocational education, your education system it's going to cost a whole lot more than it did when it was a general education system. It's not cost effective and it narrows young people's opportunities at a very young age.

VO: Education Economist and Researcher Professor Martin Gustafsson, believes this type of streaming should rather be seen as a means to redistribute opportunity.

Martin: Some technical and vocational subjects require quite high levels of competency in mathematics; computers for example. And in some ways, we are in fact pushing poorer learners very much into an academic stream because there's an absence of teachers and equipment to offer these kinds of subjects such as the engineering subjects within the secondary school system.

VO: In successful economies like Germany, industry partners with learning institutions to provide jobs and training. The DBE is making strides to collaborate with business on a number of levels.

Dr Simelane: Business and industry actually opened their training technical training centers for use by DBE to train teachers before they implement or they teach their subjects.

Stephanie: If the private sector could offer workplaces and we could rebuild our apprenticeship system that that is really important. But I think it's always going to be a very small niche sector in South Africa. The core problem is in our economy, We don't have jobs out there for all those young people.

VO: One of the positive outcomes of a Grade 9 Certificate is that it will be an earlier national benchmark, adding another layer of accountability for Principals and teachers.

Dr Ramphele: Accountability cannot be linked to examinations. Accountability is the outcome of day to day management and leadership of schools. Our problem is the quality of teaching where our teachers have insufficient content knowledge.

Dr Simelane: We are investing a lot on teacher teacher training in service but we are also recruiting bright sparks to become teachers. We are also introducing sort of a program on entrepreneurship in education

VO: The need for entrepreneurial skills is evident across the country. Soweto’s Klipspruit West Interaction Centre, co-founded by Richard De Jongh, nurtures young talent.

Richard: We started a campaign called 'It's possible' We actually drew out all the successful businesses, business owners that comes from Klipspruit west and all the successful experienced guys in their fields like your graphic designers, your I.T. industries and so on. And we brought them to the school where we started a seven week initiative

VO: One such Grade 11 pupil is Lamisha Eksteen, who attended the course and whose dream is to be a fashion designer.

Lamisha:They taught me how to sew, different techniques and this other guy also taught me entrepreneurship, what's in a business and what’s out of a business.

Mac: Before you started this course, could you sew?

Lamisha: Only by hand

Mac: How have you implemented those things practically in what you do?

Lamisha: I made a few headbands. This is one of them.

Richard: I mean she's only 16 years old. after the program she had a full fledged business, advertising and selling those already

Mac: Do you still feel the need to go through to matric because clearly you're doing what you love now

Lamisha: Even if i want to be an entrepreneur, what if it goes wrong? So then I've got a back up plan, my matric.

LINK:
Grade 9 is a crossroad for learners. Whatever academic decision they make will affect their future. So is a 14 or 15 year old equipped with the right information to make such choices?

Justine: At the age of 15 you should be responsible enough to at least think and consider these choices. I honestly think that am, but I think for a lot of other kids, they struggle.

VO: Grade 9 Pupils at Bryanston High, a former Model C school with a negligible matric drop out rate, are ambivalent about the value of the certificate.

Asante: I personally feel that getting the grade 9 certificate would be quite useless in a way because I feel like everyone has the potential to go to matric, it would open more doors for them in the future, going to college, going overseas, doing whatever they need to do.

Mac : And you Yohann?

Yohann: So for me I'm not much of a hands on person. I need my grade 12 certificate to pursue what I want to do.

VO: Principal John Skelton believes the Grade 9 certificate is a good benchmark for learners and his school is already geared up for new subjects.

John: We as a school try and cater for high academics but also for those learners who just wants to go into vocational training.

VO: The DBE's plan is ambitious - it includes introducing 22 new subjects, like plumbing and tourism from grade 8 and schools can elect what they offer. Crucially it wants to transform existing schools to cater for vocational and occupational streams, and increase the number of technical high schools.

Dr Simelane: We are looking at a 40 60 split so that the number of schools that could offer academic programs may be reduced to about 40 percent as opposed to almost a hundred percent.

Martin: Around close to half of white male matriculate for example are taking a computer subject. Those figures are down at around about 7 percent for black African students. Those kinds of inequalities are quite stark.


VO: So, the challenge for the Department is to create more equitable access to facilities in schools.


Dr Simelane: We have got a huge skills gap in the country. So these initiatives and innovations are actually meant to even address those problems that we have as a country.

Unable to find a job on his return to Johannesburg, he's now enrolled at another college to improve his qualifications. Mac: Did you always know you want to do boiler making Lindo: No I didn’t. It was a last minute option VO: Lindo really wanted to be a mechanical engineer but – like Elgin - is one of many students who may not get to follow their dream careers, because of subject choices. Juanita: My son, I know the potential that he has. So what this is actually saying to him is that he can settle for less. VO: Director of the Centre for Research and Labour at Wits University, Professor Stephanie Allais has monitored the progress of this initiative for two years and criticizes the DBE for not releasing enough information. Stephanie: If you're going to massify technical and vocational education, your education system it's going to cost a whole lot more than it did when it was a general education system. It's not cost effective and it narrows young people's opportunities at a very young age. VO: Education Economist and Researcher Professor Martin Gustafsson, believes this type of streaming should rather be seen as a means to redistribute opportunity. Martin: Some technical and vocational subjects require quite high levels of competency in mathematics; computers for example. And in some ways, we are in fact pushing poorer learners very much into an academic stream because there's an absence of teachers and equipment to offer these kinds of subjects such as the engineering subjects within the secondary school system. VO: In successful economies like Germany, industry partners with learning institutions to provide jobs and training. The DBE is making strides to collaborate with business on a number of levels. Dr Simelane: Business and industry actually opened their training technical training centers for use by DBE to train teachers before they implement or they teach their subjects. Stephanie: If the private sector could offer workplaces and we could rebuild our apprenticeship system that that is really important. But I think it's always going to be a very small niche sector in South Africa. The core problem is in our economy, We don't have jobs out there for all those young people. VO: One of the positive outcomes of a Grade 9 Certificate is that it will be an earlier national benchmark, adding another layer of accountability for Principals and teachers. Dr Ramphele: Accountability cannot be linked to examinations. Accountability is the outcome of day to day management and leadership of schools. Our problem is the quality of teaching where our teachers have insufficient content knowledge. Dr Simelane: We are investing a lot on teacher teacher training in service but we are also recruiting bright sparks to become teachers. We are also introducing sort of a program on entrepreneurship in education VO: The need for entrepreneurial skills is evident across the country. Soweto’s Klipspruit West Interaction Centre, co-founded by Richard De Jongh, nurtures young talent. Richard: We started a campaign called 'It's possible' We actually drew out all the successful businesses, business owners that comes from Klipspruit west and all the successful experienced guys in their fields like your graphic designers, your I.T. industries and so on. And we brought them to the school where we started a seven week initiative VO: One such Grade 11 pupil is Lamisha Eksteen, who attended the course and whose dream is to be a fashion designer. Lamisha:They taught me how to sew, different techniques and this other guy also taught me entrepreneurship, what's in a business and what’s out of a business. Mac: Before you started this course, could you sew? Lamisha: Only by hand Mac: How have you implemented those things practically in what you do? Lamisha: I made a few headbands. This is one of them. Richard: I mean she's only 16 years old. after the program she had a full fledged business, advertising and selling those already Mac: Do you still feel the need to go through to matric because clearly you're doing what you love now Lamisha: Even if i want to be an entrepreneur, what if it goes wrong? So then I've got a back up plan, my matric. LINK: Grade 9 is a crossroad for learners. Whatever academic decision they make will affect their future. So is a 14 or 15 year old equipped with the right information to make such choices? Justine: At the age of 15 you should be responsible enough to at least think and consider these choices. I honestly think that am, but I think for a lot of other kids, they struggle. VO: Grade 9 Pupils at Bryanston High, a former Model C school with a negligible matric drop out rate, are ambivalent about the value of the certificate. Asante: I personally feel that getting the grade 9 certificate would be quite useless in a way because I feel like everyone has the potential to go to matric, it would open more doors for them in the future, going to college, going overseas, doing whatever they need to do. Mac : And you Yohann? Yohann: So for me I'm not much of a hands on person. I need my grade 12 certificate to pursue what I want to do. VO: Principal John Skelton believes the Grade 9 certificate is a good benchmark for learners and his school is already geared up for new subjects. John: We as a school try and cater for high academics but also for those learners who just wants to go into vocational training. VO: The DBE's plan is ambitious - it includes introducing 22 new subjects, like plumbing and tourism from grade 8 and schools can elect what they offer. Crucially it wants to transform existing schools to cater for vocational and occupational streams, and increase the number of technical high schools. Dr Simelane: We are looking at a 40 60 split so that the number of schools that could offer academic programs may be reduced to about 40 percent as opposed to almost a hundred percent. Martin: Around close to half of white male matriculate for example are taking a computer subject. Those figures are down at around about 7 percent for black African students. Those kinds of inequalities are quite stark. VO: So, the challenge for the Department is to create more equitable access to facilities in schools. Dr Simelane: We have got a huge skills gap in the country. So these initiatives and innovations are actually meant to even address those problems that we have as a country.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): A General Education Certificate at the end of Grade 9 has educators polarised, highlighting a system that is fundamentally broken at the core. Will this certificate add value to our children’s futur
metadata.Unique Selling Point: By the end of July 2020 the field trial for the general education certificate at the end of Grade 9 is scheduled for completion. Not an exit strategy for learners according to the Department of Education, rather opening the options for non academic streams as well as setting an earlier national benchmark for learners before they get to Grade 12. But can this certificate enhance a failing educational system in dire need of attention?
metadata.Summary: A Grade 9 certificate for South African learners is on the horizon. It is meant to create alternative learning streams for pupils not necessarily wanting to follow an academic outcome for their education, as well as providing an early national benchmark making schools accountable in earlier grades. This is modelled on the German schooling system, but South Africa has very different challenges when it comes to education infrastructure and industry participation which forms a large part of the German model. A recent study has outlined fundamental failings within our education system with; 20% absenteeism of teachers on Mondays and Fridays, rising to 33% at every month-end, in schools serving predominantly poor black children only an average of 3.5 hours per school day is spent teaching compared to 6.5 hours in the middle and upper-class schools. According to critics of the new certificate, many challenges across the country, including the observation that Grade 4 children have not yet learned to read with meaning need to be addressed before a grade 9 certificate enters our educational framework. In addition, many educators say that this Grade 9 certificate is going to be costly to implement, in terms of infrastructure, implementation and resources - including supplying teachers who are skilled enough to teach the myriad of new subjects that will be introduced into schools. With the introduction of these subjects it may even be duplicating what the system has currently in place, in terms of the TVET colleges that are supposed to accommodate the non academic stream towards a National Certificate. On the other hand, the Department believes that this certificate will give more credence to the TVET qualifications. Is the new Grade 9 certificate a deflection from the perception that, educationally, South Africa is moving backwards?
metadata.Further information: We explore the pros and cons of this certificate whilst highlighting the plight of many young people as they face the crossroads of their academic pathway when they reach Grade 9. Do they continue to struggle on with an academic pathway if they are not doing well at school or do they choose the vocation or occupational streams that will now provide new options for them? Professor Allais believes that the option of a non academic pathway that is being presented as a serious option is not the answer. She says that, because we are educating our children poorly we are creating options, such that, we don’t have to get the fundamentals of our educational system right first. If pupils were being taught properly to start off with then these would not necessarily be options they would follow. According to her, the world trend is to move away from an early certification. Professor Stephanie Allais is fundamentally opposed to the Grade 9 certificate and is afraid that as a consequence, learners may take the easy way out of the school system, or be forced to follow alternative streams if their marks do not meet the grade, meaning we are not giving many learners a chance to improve their circumstance. According to her it perpetuates the cycle of poverty and class differentiation. She also says that for a model like this to work as it does in Germany and even Sweden, there needs to be industry involvement with curriculum setting and provision of apprenticeships and jobs. In South Africa we are nowhere near that. Dr Ramphele asserts, “The question we should be asking ourselves as a society is why after 25 years of poor quality education outcomes we are still struggling to confront the root causes of this tragedy? Is there perhaps a mindset that propels us to have low expectations of our children, our teachers and ourselves?” We also speak to two schools, Randburg Hoerskool and Klipspruit. Kipspruit has been at the brink of closing down, and with community involvement by a local group they have organised a course where the pupils are exposed to alternative career paths in a vocational and occupational sense. They did this to inspire learners to continue with their studies and not drop out of school. This is the department’s argument that, because there is such a high drop-out rate before Grade 12, this 3 tiered streaming will encourage pupils to stay in school. We interview a young TVET graduate, who is still battling to find work and, along with 7 siblings, lives with his grandmother who is a teacher. We speak to a Grade 9 pupil who is at the point of choosing their way forward. He wants to follow a non academic path but his mother is adamant that he has to do an academic matric. We also speak to a pupil who attended the 7 week Klipspruit workshop and get some insight into how it changed the way they perceive their options after finishing school, now that they have been exposed to vocational and occupational subjects. Richard De Jongh is the initiator of this workshop and an example of how community intervention can play a role in changing a school’s outcomes. We also get to speak to the principal of Klipspruit. At Randburg Hoerskool, we will get the alternative narrative of a school with more means and speak to the principal, Pieter Booysen on what the Grade 9 certificate will mean to a more academically inclined school and it’s pupils. Dr Ramphele poses some solution and issues that need to be addressed first. She gives examples of community involvement as well as looking at performance based pay for teachers, which has worked well in places like India and Singapore, so that we start improving the system at the core. Home language based education needs to be part of the way forward, and improving literacy and numeracy at early grades. According to Professor Allais who has been monitoring the progress of this Grade 9 certificate for the last two years, there has been very little discussion and participation from the DBE with regards to exploring the certificate’s merits prior to implementation. We challenge the Department and try to get some clarity on the burning issues.
